title: Short-Term Abstinence Reveals Hematological, Biochemical, and Gene–Protein Profile Changes in Methamphetamine and Ice Users
description: Addictive substances are a critical public health problem in Thailand and worldwide. Methamphetamine and ice (MI) are frequently used to enhance alertness and prolong working hours by directly affecting the central nervous system and other organs. This study aimed to identify biomarkers for current MI users (MIB) and individuals after 20 days of abstinence (MIA) Compared with healthy controls, MI use increased red blood cell (RBC) and platelet (PLT) counts, did not affect total white blood cell (WBC) numbers, but increased the proportion of neutrophils while decreasing lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, and basophils. Short-term MI abstinence did not substantially alter hematological or biochemical parameters, except for an increase in alanine aminotransferase (ALT). MIB showed impaired neutrophil phagocytosis and reduced bactericidal activity via the respiratory burst. In MIA, respiratory burst activity was partially restored but remained lower than in healthy controls. Transcriptomic analysis identified CEACAM4, IFIT2, KCNJ2, FRAT2, and RNF139 as a candidate mRNA biomarker panel for MIA. Serum proteomic analysis revealed distinct protein profiles between methamphetamine-only users and MI users, indicating differential systemic effects between these groups. In conclusion, MI impairs hematological parameters and neutrophil function. Both mRNA and protein biomarkers may be useful for monitoring abstinence status during rehabilitation. Overall design: Whole blood samples from methamphetamine (ice) users undergoing drug rehabilitation at Thanyarak Songkhla Hospital, Songkhla Province, were collected at two time points. Time point 1 was at day 0, when patients tested positive for methamphetamine in urine (MIB). Time point 2 was at day 20, when the same patients had abstained from addictive substances for 20 days (MIA). Hematological parameters (CBC), biochemical parameters of methamphetamine users (MIB and MIA) were obtained from Thunyarak Songkhla Hospital. While these parameters of healthy control were obtained from Walailak University Hospital. Whole blood of MIB, MIA and healthy control obtained from Thunyarak Songkhla Hospital. Hematological parameters, including red blood cell count, white blood cell count, platelet count, and the percentages of neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, and basophils, were compared among healthy controls, MIB, and MIA groups. Biochemical parameters included liver function tests (AST, ALT, albumin, total protein, globulin, total bilirubin, and direct bilirubin), kidney function tests (creatinine and BUN), and serum electrolytes (Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻, and CO₂). These parameters were compared between MIB and MIA groups. Only ALT was found to be significantly increased in the MIA group compared with the MIB group. RNA from whole blood of MIB and MIA were examined using RNA sequencing technology. A total of 25 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified with 10 DEGs upregulated and 15 DEGs downregulated in MIA compared with MIB (Figure 2A). The DEGs were shown in heatmap and volcano plot (Figure 2B-C). None of gene ontology was classified from these DEGs. The nine candidate genes, CEACAM4, IFIT2, KCNJ2, FRAT2, PCK2, KATA6B, RNF139, ZBTB4, and PARN, were validated by qPCR. The mRNA levels of CEACAM4, IFIT2, KCNJ2, FRAT2 and RNF139 mRNA levels were downregulated in MIA (Figures 4D). The other genes levels were unchanged Whole blood from healthy controls, MIB, and MIA groups was incubated with Escherichia coli or Candida albicans at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 10:1 for 2 and 3 hours, respectively. The percentage of phagocytic neutrophils was assessed using blood smears. Both MIB and MIA groups exhibited reduced phagocytic activity compared with healthy controls. Cells were further incubated with nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) to evaluate the respiratory burst. The percentage of NBT-positive neutrophils was examined using blood smears. NBT-positive neutrophils were almost undetectable in the MIB group; this percentage was increased in the MIA group but remained lower than that of healthy controls.
